name: palette-control
description: Doc 67 slate item E. THE CONTROL ARM for palette-cliff.json: the same fifteen NPC positions in the same order on the same map, but drawn from the four stock NPC palettes -- which is what a real Emerald crowd looks like. Cold boot with nothing held. Measured: 7/16 slots used, 0 mis-served object events. A single crowded map coming back mis-coloured would be equally consistent with 'one of those graphics is broken'; this arm is what rules that out (doc 61 sec.4). Generated by make_palettes.py --specs; do not hand-edit.
symbols_from_why: gPalProbe* exist only in this fork; a run against the pinned engine would fail to resolve them. The maps exist only here too.

probes.why: Doc 66's rule -- assert the thing under test actually happened. A palette table read on the wrong screen is a measurement of a different screen.
gMapHeader.mapLayoutId. WHICH ARM the boot-key selector chose. Without this a green run on the control map would be reported as a green run on the cliff map.

gPalProbeActive -- live object events including the player. 16 means the object-event budget is exactly full, which is what makes 15 the most NPCs a map can show and therefore what bounds this experiment.
gPalProbeSlotsUsed -- how many of the 16 sprite palette slots hold a tag.

gPalProbeMismatch -- THE DELIVERABLE. Active object events whose sprite points at a palette slot holding a tag that is not their own. This is the failure stated as a number; the picture is what shows it is not merely a number.
gPalProbeOnSlot15 -- how many landed specifically on slot 15, where CreateSprite's 0xFF truncates to in a 4-bit bitfield.

gPalProbeLoadFails, latched inside LoadSpritePalette itself. The CAUSE, recorded at the point of refusal, independently of the consequence -- 'an NPC is wearing the wrong colours' has more than one possible cause and this rules the others out.
gPalProbeLastFailTag -- WHICH palette was refused. Names the victim instead of counting victims.
sSpritePaletteTags[15]. What the mis-coloured NPCs are actually wearing.

gPalProbeWantTag[15] -- the palette the LAST object event slot's graphic asks for. Object events are first-fit from slot 0 with the player in slot 0, so this is the last template on the map: the one at the back of the queue when the allocator runs dry.

gPalProbeGotTag[15] -- the palette it is actually being drawn with. want_last and got_last disagreeing IS the finding, named rather than counted: not 'two sprites are wrong' but 'this one wanted X and is wearing Y'.

assert.why: CONTROL. Shared by both arms; must be green in both, which is what aims a failure at the palettes rather than at the boot.
CONTROL. This run is on PalControl, layout id 442.
CONTROL. 15 NPCs + the player. Shared by both arms: if this differs between them the crowd is not identical and nothing downstream compares.
How full the palette table got. Exact, not a threshold: doc 55 sec.9.4's list makes in_range and >= weak under an address shift.
THE DISCRIMINATOR, from the control side. Zero here and non-zero on the cliff arm is what makes the finding a property of palette DIVERSITY rather than of crowding.
Where the refused sprites landed. Names the mechanism (a 4-bit truncation of 0xFF) rather than just its size.
The cause, counted at the point of refusal.
The palette the last-spawned NPC's graphic asks for.
It gets what it asked for. Equal to want_last, which is what a correct run looks like.
